t: Minimum Path Cost in a Grid
o: Start anywhere in row 0, end anywhere in the last row; each step moves from a cell (any column) to any cell in the next row, paying moveCost[cellValue][destCol] plus the destination cell's own value. Path cost = sum of all visited cell values + all move costs. With m,n ≤ 50, an O(m·n²) DP is trivial. Example 1: path 5→0→1 costs 5+0+1 + moveCost[5][0](=3... per statement 3) + moveCost[0][1](=8) = 17.
k: dp[i][j] = min cost of a path starting in row 0 and ending at cell (i,j), including all cell values and moves.
Transition: dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min over k of dp[i-1][k] + moveCost[grid[i-1][k]][j].
Only the previous row matters, so a rolling 1D array suffices.

a.i: Initialize dp with row 0's values. For each subsequent row, every column j takes the cheapest predecessor from the row above, adding the move cost indexed by the predecessor's cell value plus its own value. The answer is the min of the last row.
s: dp = copy of grid[0]; pv = copy of grid[0] (previous row's values).
For each row i ≥ 1: ndp[j] = grid[i][j] + min_k(dp[k] + moveCost[pv[k]][j]).
a.t: O(m·n²) — for each of m rows and n columns we scan n predecessors.
a.sp: O(n) for the rolling DP rows.

w: The subtle bug source is indexing moveCost by the previous cell's *value*, not its coordinates — that's why we carry pv alongside dp. Since grid holds distinct values 0..mn-1, moveCost lookup is direct. Follow-ups: reconstruct the actual path (keep parent pointers), or handle weighted transitions requiring Dijkstra if movement weren't layer-restricted.
